newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Campers warned as next cyclone nears New Zealand.
newsitem.headline: Campers warned as next cyclone nears New Zealand.

text.p: New Zealand weather forecasters warned campers to pack up and flee on Thursday as the country braced for its second tropical storm in two weeks at the height of the summer holiday season.

The Meteorological Service said Cyclone Drena would bear down on the North Island on Friday, bringing winds of up to 130 km/hour (80 miles/hour) and dumping up to 350 mm (14 inches) of rain in less than 24 hours.
"We're talking about a major cyclone event ... This is a dangerous storm," chief forecaster Augie Auer said.
He warned campers to beat a retreat from resorts in the upper North Island and Coromandel Peninsula, which took a battering late last month from the remnants of Cyclone Fergus.

"Coromandel will cop it again. You might get away with spending another night in the Coromandel before you have to move out tomorrow morning, but that's cutting it pretty close and if it were me, I'd be moving out as well," Auer said.

Auer said the cyclone would track down the west of the country and have a greater impact than Fergus on populous areas, including New Zealand's biggest city, Auckland. The motorway bridge across Auckland Harbour could be dangerous as winds of around 90 km/hour (56 miles/hour) buffeted the city.
Civil Defence director Paul Officer issued a warning to all holidaymakers of "the significant dangers that high winds and heavy rainfall can bring".
He said air and road travel could be disrupted.
Campground operators in the north of the country bemoaned their misfortune as a fresh exodus of holidaymakers began.
"Some of them are shipping out today, some tomorrow... They're clearing out fast," said Sue Campbell, a holiday park manager in the Bay of Islands, one of New Zealand's top tourist destinations.
"We've lost a lot of money, just like everybody else."
Cyclone Fergus, downgraded to a deep depression as it hit New Zealand on December 30, caused landslips and flooding and prompted some local councils to declare a state of emergency.
But there were no major casualties, and some holidaymakers accused weather forecasters of sowing unnecessary panic.
